Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Bookings API

The Bookings API lets your application create, move, and cancel appointments on a shared calendar without touching the underlying calendar provider directly. It handles the parts that are tedious to get right: overlapping holds, time zones that shift under daylight saving, and two clients trying to claim the same 10:00 slot within a few milliseconds of each other.

Everything is organised around three resources. A *calendar* is the bookable thing, whether that is a person, a meeting room, or a piece of equipment. An *availability rule* describes when that calendar can be booked, in recurring weekly blocks plus one-off exceptions. A *booking* is a confirmed claim on a span of time, and it always belongs to exactly one calendar. Those three cover every endpoint in the reference.

Requests and responses are JSON, timestamps are RFC 3339 with an explicit offset, and every write endpoint accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header so that a retried request after a network timeout does not produce a duplicate booking. Read the conventions page once and you can skip the boilerplate in every later section.

This guide starts with authentication and a first booking you can make in about five minutes. From there it covers availability queries, recurrence, webhooks for cancellations made outside your app, and the error codes you will hit in production.

If you are migrating from v1, start with the migration notes instead. The slot model changed, and the old `/slots/reserve` call has no direct equivalent.

Add a paragraph on authentication.

output: Authentication uses a bearer token sent in the `Authorization` header. Tokens are scoped per calendar set, so a token issued for the sales team's calendars returns 403 on a booking that belongs to support. Create tokens in the dashboard under Settings, API keys; each one carries an explicit scope list such as `bookings:write` or `availability:read`, and a token missing the scope an endpoint needs fails with `error.code` set to `insufficient_scope` rather than a generic 401. Server-side calls should use a secret key. For browser or mobile clients, mint a short-lived client token from your backend instead, since it expires in 15 minutes and cannot list calendars it was not granted. Rotating a key does not invalidate the old one immediately: both stay valid for 24 hours so you can redeploy without dropped requests.
